name: Storing money amounts
needs: my totals are off by a cent
0.1 plus 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in my invoice
how should I save prices in the database
summary: Keeping money exact. Store amounts as whole minor units (cents) in an integer column, or as a fixed DECIMAL, always next to a currency code. Never use floating point for money, and round once, at a defined step.
need_when: Your app shows, adds up or charges any price, fee, balance or split.
skip_when: Never. Even one price field benefits from getting this right on day one.

ways.title: Integer minor units
ways.how: amount_cents BIGINT plus currency CHAR(3), the same shape Stripe's API uses. Convert to display format only at the edge.
ways.tradeoff: Exact and fast. Currencies with 0 or 3 decimals need a lookup table.

ways.title: DECIMAL columns and decimal types
ways.how: NUMERIC(12,2) in the database and Python Decimal, Java BigDecimal or a library like dinero.js in code.
ways.tradeoff: Readable values. Every language boundary (JSON, JavaScript) must avoid floats.

ways.title: A money library
ways.how: dinero.js (JavaScript), py-moneyed or django-money (Python), the money gem (Ruby) bundle amount and currency with safe math.

prompt:
Fix how my app stores and calculates money.

Requirements:
- Find every money field and every place money is calculated.
- Store amounts as [integer minor units in a BIGINT] with a currency code column (ISO 4217). No float or double anywhere.
- Do math in integers or a decimal type. Round once, with a named rule ([half up / banker's]), at a defined step such as per line item.
- When splitting amounts (for example 100 into 3), give the leftover cent to a defined party so parts always add up to the total.
- Send amounts in APIs as integers with currency, never as floats.
- Format for display with the user's locale only in the UI.
- Write a migration that converts existing data exactly, and tests for rounding and splits.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. Searching the schema and code finds no float columns or float math on money.
2. Splitting $100.00 three ways gives parts that add to exactly $100.00.
3. A yen price has no decimals and a dollar price has two.
4. Totals match the payment provider's to the cent across 1,000 test orders.
5. JSON responses carry integers, not 19.990000000001.
acceptance_checks: Searching the schema and code finds no float columns or float math on money.
Splitting $100.00 three ways gives parts that add to exactly $100.00.
A yen price has no decimals and a dollar price has two.
Totals match the payment provider's to the cent across 1,000 test orders.
if_you_skip_it: Invoices and payouts drift by cents, reports never reconcile with the payment provider, and support gets "you overcharged me" emails.
